title: H3 Hex Index Helper: Hexagonal Spatial Index
description: Use coordinates as the basis for H3 hexagonal indexing workflows with the H3 Hex Index Helper — resolutions and cell sizes explained. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, H3 resolution 9 cells average about 0.105 km² — city-block scale — while resolution 7's 5.16 km² cells swallow neighbourhoods whole; choosing the resolution is choosing the analysis.
quick_answer: The H3 Hex Index Helper uses coordinates as the basis for hexagonal spatial index workflows — Uber's H3 system of nested hexagon cells addressed by a single index. Enter a point and work with its cell — the modern alternative to square grids, with every neighbour at one distance.

The table on this page maps resolutions 0–15 to average cell areas — the choice that decides whether your analysis sees blocks or boroughs.
Rings around a cell (k-ring) are uniform in hexagons — surge zones and catchments drawn in cell steps behave the same in every direction.
Publish counts per cell instead of points: pick a resolution whose cells hold enough people to be safe, using the area table as the guide.
A square cell has two neighbour distances (edge and corner); a hexagon has one. Movement, spread and diffusion models stop lying about diagonals the day they switch to hexagons.

A hexagon grid cannot tile a sphere perfectly — H3 inherits exactly 12 pentagon cells from its icosahedron base, one famously in the Atlantic. Every H3 user meets them eventually; the helper's framing prepares you.

faq: Is this the Uber H3 library?

It is a helper for H3-based workflows — the concepts, resolutions and indexing approach of Uber's open-source H3. Production pipelines should use the official H3 libraries for their language; this page is the understanding and spot-checking layer.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84, the frame web maps and GPS share — tile and pixel systems on this page are defined over it.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — pixels and tiles quantise the world; extra coordinate decimals beyond the cell size are decoration.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
H3 indexes paste as identifiers; QGIS and most geo stacks have H3 plugins or libraries to render cells from indexes.
H3 versus geohash?
Hexagons versus rectangles: uniform neighbours versus prefix simplicity. Geohash wins on string tricks, H3 wins on spatial statistics — many stacks use both.
H3 versus S2?
Google's S2 (squares on a cube-sphere) is the other modern system. The choice is ecosystem: H3's analytics community versus S2's geometry rigour.
Are cells exactly equal-area?
Nearly — areas vary a few percent across the globe, far tighter than latitude-longitude grids. 'Average' in the table is honest wording.
What is a k-ring?
All cells within k steps of a centre cell — the hexagon's clean neighbourhood, with (3k(k+1)+1) cells: 7 at k=1, 19 at k=2.
Pentagons break things?
Pentagon cells have 5 neighbours instead of 6; libraries handle them, algorithms should be told. Twelve exist, always — sphere geometry's tax.
Point to cell is many-to-one?
Deliberately — indexing trades the point for its cell, the foundation of aggregation and privacy uses.
Hierarchies?
Each cell has a parent at the next coarser resolution (roughly 7 children per parent) — the tree that rollups are built on.
